explanations.answer: The way to walk and what to do
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. They ask Jeremiah to pray that the LORD will tell them "the way we should walk and the thing we should do." They want directions, and they say they'll follow them. I think a lot of us would sign up for that before breakfast.

explanations.answer: How long Babylon will rule them
explanations.explanation: Good guess, since Babylon is on everybody's mind here. But they never ask about timelines. They ask Jeremiah to pray that the LORD will tell them "the way we should walk and the thing we should do." They're asking what to do next, not how long Babylon will be around.

explanations.answer: Who their next governor will be
explanations.explanation: Makes sense, friend, with Gedaliah, the governor Babylon appointed, gone. But the people don't ask for a new governor. They ask Jeremiah to pray that the LORD will tell them "the way we should walk and the thing we should do." They want a direction for their feet.
True, baker! Jeremiah tells them, "I will not withhold a word from you." He also says he'll pray as they ask and tell them everything the LORD answers. Nothing gets trimmed off the edges.
It's actually true, friend. Jeremiah says plainly, "I will not withhold a word from you." He promises to tell them everything the LORD answers. No pinching off the dough before it gets to them.

explanations.answer: Make it go well with them
explanations.explanation: Right on, baker. They say they'll obey so that "it may go well with us when we obey the voice of the LORD our God!" They're even saying it before they hear the answer, pleasant or unpleasant. That's a big promise to make with the oven door still shut.

I see why you'd go there, since Ishmael just caused all that trouble. But the people don't mention him here. They say obeying is "so that it may go well with us." It's the whole picture they have in mind, not just one man.

Close to the mood, friend, since the king of Babylon is on their minds. But the people never say a word about earning favor. They say they'll obey "so that it may go well with us." Their hope is for things to go well, not for a pat on the back from a king.

That's the one, baker. The LORD says, "If you will indeed stay in this land, then I will build you up and not tear you down." The offer is on the table, and it starts with staying put. Simple, but I think staying put is harder than it sounds when you're scared.
Not quite, friend. Nobody is asked to fight anybody here. The LORD says, "If you will indeed stay in this land, then I will build you up and not tear you down." The word is stay.

I can see how you landed there, since folks are scared. But the LORD doesn't say hide. He says, "If you will indeed stay in this land, then I will build you up and not tear you down." Staying in the open is a different thing than hiding.
Yes, baker. The LORD says, "Do not be afraid of the king of Babylon, whom you now fear." He even says it twice in a row, like He wants it to sink in. When God repeats Himself, I lean in.
Good try, friend, but that's not the word. The LORD says, "Do not be afraid of the king of Babylon, whom you now fear." Fear is what they're carrying, and that's what He speaks to.
Nope, nobody's jealous of anybody here, baker. The LORD says, "Do not be afraid of the king of Babylon, whom you now fear." The problem is fear, plain and simple.

explanations.answer: He is with them to save them
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The LORD says, "for I am with you to save you and deliver you from him." The reason not to be afraid is not a changed situation, it's who is with them. That's a better reason than any I ever had in the dark.

explanations.answer: The king's army has gone home
explanations.explanation: Reasonable thought, friend, but the LORD says nothing about an army leaving. His reason is, "for I am with you to save you and deliver you from him." The comfort is His presence, not an empty road.

explanations.answer: The king has made peace with them
explanations.explanation: I get it, since He does mention the king showing compassion later. But that's not the reason given here. The LORD says, "for I am with you to save you and deliver you from him." The reason is that He is with them.

explanations.answer: Being restored to their own land
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! The LORD says, "And I will show you compassion, and he will have compassion on you and restore you to your own land." Compassion and a way back home, together. That's a good box of news.
Not this one, friend. The LORD says the king "will have compassion on you and restore you to your own land." It's their own land, not a new spot in Babylon (Jeremiah 42:12).

explanations.answer: Being given a king of their own
explanations.explanation: Interesting pick, baker, but the LORD doesn't promise a king here. He says the king of Babylon "will have compassion on you and restore you to your own land." What comes with the compassion is the land.
That's right, baker. The second if has them saying, "No, but we will go to the land of Egypt and live there." Egypt is the place they picture for a fresh start.
Not Moab, friend. Moab is a neighboring land, but the LORD names a different one. He pictures them saying, "we will go to the land of Egypt and live there."
Edom is another neighbor, but it's not the one here, baker. The second if has them saying, "No, but we will go to the land of Egypt and live there." Egypt is the answer.
Right, baker. They picture Egypt as a place "where we will not see war or hear the sound of the ram's horn or hunger for bread." War and hunger are the two things they want to leave behind.
Reasonable, friend, but that's not on their list. They picture Egypt as a place "where we will not see war or hear the sound of the ram's horn or hunger for bread." It's war and hunger.
Nice try, baker, but weather isn't mentioned. They picture Egypt as a place "where we will not see war or hear the sound of the ram's horn or hunger for bread." That's war and hunger.

That's it, baker. The LORD says "the sword you fear will overtake you there, and the famine you dread will follow on your heels into Egypt." The very things they're running from catch up with them. Like trying to outrun your own shadow, and I've tried.
That's the hope the people have, friend, but it's not what the LORD says. He says "the famine you dread will follow on your heels into Egypt." It doesn't stay behind.

No, baker. Nothing in the LORD's word turns the sword and famine on Babylon. He says "the sword you fear will overtake you there, and the famine you dread will follow on your heels into Egypt." They follow the remnant.

True, baker. The LORD says, "Not one of them will survive or escape the disaster I will bring upon them." That's about all who resolve to go to Egypt to live there. It's a heavy line, and I think it's meant to be taken seriously.

It's actually true, friend. The LORD says of those who resolve to go to Egypt, "Not one of them will survive or escape the disaster I will bring upon them." It's a heavy word, and the text doesn't soften it.
Yes, baker. The LORD says, "you will never see this place again." That's the land they're standing in as Jeremiah speaks. It's a sober line, so I'll leave it right there.
Not Babylon, friend. They were never headed there, and the LORD doesn't name it. He says, "you will never see this place again," meaning the land where they are now.
Good thinking, since Egypt has the Nile, but that's the place they're going, not the place they'll lose. The LORD says, "you will never see this place again." He means the land they're in now.

That's the word, baker. Jeremiah says, "For you have deceived yourselves by sending me to the LORD your God." They said they'd do whatever the LORD said, and Jeremiah says they've fooled themselves. I think that's the hardest kind of fooling.
Nope, friend. Jeremiah doesn't say they honored themselves. He says, "For you have deceived yourselves by sending me to the LORD your God." It's a sharp word, but it's the one in the text.
Not protected, baker. Jeremiah says, "For you have deceived yourselves by sending me to the LORD your God." He's pointing at the gap between what they promised and what they're doing.
Not quite, friend. Jeremiah says the opposite: "you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD your God in all He has sent me to tell you." So the answer is false. He's telling them they haven't obeyed.

Right, baker. Jeremiah says, "you have not obeyed the voice of the LORD your God in all He has sent me to tell you." He's not praising them, he's pointing out they haven't done it. It's a hard thing to hear, and I think he said it plainly on purpose.
